Empirical Research Plan: “Bank Mergers and Local Crime”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Strategy: Staggered-adoption Difference-in-Differences (DID) complemented with an event-study.

Why appropriate  
• The “treatment” (a merger that changes local banking competition) occurs at specific, observable dates that vary by county between 1990-2000 → classic staggered policy adoption setting.  
• Counties not exposed to any in-market merger over the sample window provide a natural counterfactual.  
• County crime is observed annually for many years before and after the event, allowing pre-trend tests and dynamic effect estimation.  
• Institutional details (federal approval process, long lags between announcement and consummation) support the view that exact consummation dates are plausibly exogenous to short-run county-level shocks, strengthening the DID design.

Implementation: Two-way fixed effects (county and year) as a starting point; primary estimates based on Callaway-Sant’Anna (2021) or Sun & Abraham (2021) estimators to avoid bias from heterogeneous treatment timing. An event-study (-5 to +8 years relative to merger) is reported for pre-trend diagnostics and dynamic impacts.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
Treated = 1 for county c in year t if, by t, a consummated bank-bank merger in which BOTH banks previously maintained branches in county c has increased the local deposit-weighted Herfindahl–Hirschman Index (HHI) by ≥ 100 points (DOJ’s material-change threshold). After the first qualifying merger, treatment remains 1 thereafter (“ever-treated”).

Control group  
Counties that (i) never experience such an in-market merger during 1990-2000 OR (ii) only experience mergers where the HHI rise < 100 (placebo counties).  
Robustness: nearest-neighbor propensity-score matched controls and border-county controls.

Treatment timing / event date  
The effective date of merger consummation listed in the FDIC Summary of Deposits (SoD) and Federal Reserve merger approval files. Year t* is the first calendar year containing at least six post-merger months; treatment starts in t*.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends: Absent a merger, crime trends in treated and control counties would have evolved similarly.  
Plausibility: Tests of pre-treatment slopes in the event-study plus covariate balance (unemployment, demographics, pre-merger crime level) will be shown.

A2. No time-varying unobservables correlated with both merger timing and crime.  
Plausibility: Federal approval decisions depend mainly on bank finances/competition, not short-run local crime. County×year controls (unemployment, income, police force size) help.

A3. Stable treatment (SUTVA): a county’s crime is affected only by its own mergers.  
Plausibility: Some spillovers are possible (residents travel for loans, criminals cross borders) but most banking relationships are local. We add MSA-year FEs and drop border counties in a robustness test.

A4. No anticipation: Crime does not react to the announcement earlier than the consummation date.  
Plausibility: Households and potential offenders likely learn credit terms after branches consolidate, not at announcement. We add leads in the event-study to verify.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Selective merger timing into counties on worsening economic trajectories.  
Fix: Include county-specific linear trends; control for time-varying county economics; show parallel pre-trends.

T2. Spillovers to neighboring (control) counties.  
Fix: Drop counties within 25 miles of any treated county (“donut” sample); alternatively aggregate to CZ (commuting zone) level.

T3. Multiple overlapping mergers (treatment re-dosage).  
Fix: Define treatment as first major HHI-increasing merger; control for a “post-second-merger” dummy; use cumulative HHI change as continuous treatment in robustness.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# --------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)     # fast data handling
library(fixest)         # fast fixed-effects estimators
library(did)            # Callaway & Sant’Anna DID
library(ggplot2)

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load data
# --------------------------------------------------------------
crime   <- fread("county_crime_1990_2000.csv")      # FBI UCR
mergers <- fread("bank_mergers_1990_2000.csv")      # FDIC / Fed
socdem  <- fread("county_covariates.csv")           # BEA, Census

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Construct treatment
# --------------------------------------------------------------
# Step 1: compute within-county HHI change for each merger
mergers[, hhi_change := post_hhi - pre_hhi]

# Step 2: keep only “material” mergers
mergers_t <- mergers[hhi_change >= 100]

# Step 3: first qualifying merger date by county
first_merge <- mergers_t[order(consummation_date),
                         .(merge_date = min(consummation_date)),
                         by = county_fips]

# Step 4: create panel with treatment dummy
panel <- merge(crime, socdem, by = c("county_fips","year"), all.x = TRUE)
panel <- merge(panel, first_merge, by = "county_fips", all.x = TRUE)

panel[, treat := 0]
panel[!is.na(merge_date) & year >= year(merge_date), treat := 1]

# Event-time
panel[, rel_year := year - year(merge_date)]
panel[is.na(rel_year), rel_year := -999]  # untreated

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main TWFE specification
# --------------------------------------------------------------
fe_reg <- feols(log1p(total_crime) ~ treat + unem_rate + median_income +
                    police_officers_percap | county_fips + year,
                data = panel, cluster = ~county_fips)

summary(fe_reg)

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Callaway–Sant’Anna estimator (robust to timing)
# --------------------------------------------------------------
cs_out <- att_gt(yname = "log1p(total_crime)",
                 tname = "year",
                 idname = "county_fips",
                 gname = "merge_year",      # first treated year
                 xformla = ~ unem_rate + median_income +
                            police_officers_percap,
                 data = panel)

agg_effect <- aggte(cs_out, type = "simple")
summary(agg_effect)

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Event study plot
# --------------------------------------------------------------
es <- feols(log1p(total_crime) ~ i(rel_year, ref = -1) +
             unem_rate + median_income +
             police_officers_percap |
             county_fips + year,
             data = panel[rel_year >= -5 & rel_year <= 8])

iplot(es, xlab = "Years since merger", ylab = "Log crime β")

# --------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. Robustness: Donut-sample excluding neighbors
# --------------------------------------------------------------
border <- fread("county_neighbors.csv")  # id neighbor counties
treated_ctys <- unique(first_merge$county_fips)
border[, near_treated := neighbor_fips %in% treated_ctys]
drop_ctys <- unique(border[near_treated == TRUE]$county_fips)

panel_donut <- panel[!county_fips %in% drop_ctys]
feols(log1p(total_crime) ~ treat + unem_rate + median_income |
      county_fips + year, data = panel_donut, cluster = ~county_fips)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Economic intuition: By reducing local credit competition, mergers tighten credit supply for marginal households/firms, hampering legal economic opportunities and potentially raising property crime. Violent crime could also rise via general economic stress but likely by less.

Prior: A major merger raises total crime by roughly 3–5 percent (≈ 0.03–0.05 log points) within three years, concentrated in property offenses (burglary, larceny).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Pre-treatment parallel trends verified (event-study, covariate balance) …… 1  
C2: Exogeneity of treatment timing given observables & controls …………………… 0.8  
C3: No significant spillovers across counties ………………………………………… 0.5  
C4: No anticipation effects (leads ≈ 0) ………………………………………………… 0.9  
C5: Correct estimator for staggered timing / heterogeneous effects ……………… 1  

Overall average ≈ 0.84 → design is fairly credible but relies on managing spillovers.
